title: Staircase Search in a Sorted Table
statement:
You get an m × n table of integers. Every row is sorted in ascending order from left to right, and every column is sorted in ascending order from top to bottom. Values may repeat.

Return true if target appears anywhere in the table, and false otherwise.

The rows do not continue each other. The last value of a row can be larger than the first value of the next row, so you cannot treat the table as one long sorted list.

examples.why: 12 sits in the bottom row. Note that row 0 ends with 11 while row 1 starts with 4: the table is not sorted as one flat list.
10 would fit between 9 and 11, but no cell holds it. Even an absent value forces you to rule out every row and column.
A single row: the target is the last cell.

constraints: Every row and every column is sorted ascending
hints: Pick a corner of the table where one step in one direction makes values bigger and a step in the other makes them smaller.
Start at the top-right cell. If it is bigger than the target, the whole column below it is bigger too. If it is smaller, the whole row to its left is smaller too.
Each comparison throws away one full row or one full column, so you walk a staircase of at most m + n steps.

explain.intuition:
Stand on the top-right cell. Everything to its left in that row is smaller, everything below it in that column is bigger. So one comparison settles a whole line: if the cell is bigger than target, nothing below it can match, so drop the column and step left. If it is smaller, nothing to its left can match, so drop the row and step down.

Each step removes a row or a column, so after at most m + n steps you either land on the target or walk off the table. The bottom-left corner works the same way, mirrored. The top-left corner does not: from there both moves make values bigger, so a comparison tells you nothing about which way to go.
steps: While row < m and col ≥ 0, look at v = table[row][col].
If v > target, move left (col--); otherwise move down (row++).
If you leave the table, return false.
pitfalls: Flattening the table and running one binary search. That only works when each row starts after the previous one ends, which this table does not promise.
Starting at the top-left or bottom-right corner, where both moves go in the same direction and nothing can be ruled out.
Binary searching on the diagonal alone. It narrows things down but still leaves two sub-tables to search.

solutions.title: Check every cell
Binary search each row
solutions.idea: Every row is sorted, so run a binary search on each one. Skip rows whose range cannot contain the target.

solutions.title: Staircase walk from the top-right corner
solutions.idea: Each comparison rules out a whole row or a whole column.

followups: Count how many cells are smaller than or equal to target, still in O(m + n).
Find the k-th smallest value in the table. How does the staircase count help a binary search on the value?
